stories.topic: Sara Rai's Astonishing Powers of Observation
stories.summary: Amit once asked Sara Rai (writer and Munshi Premchand's granddaughter) how she remembered so much from her childhood — her recollections were so precise they felt like beautifully crafted fiction. She replied simply: 'We had nothing else to do. So we looked at things.' In the 70s and 80s, with no scrolling and no constant sensation, attention had to land somewhere — usually on the world.
stories.insight: Attention is the substrate of memory, and attention has a budget. When the environment offers infinite cheap stimulation, the budget gets shredded into fragments; when it offers little, it pools into deep observation. The trade isn't free — modern abundance has a hidden cost in the texture and density of our remembered lives.

stories.topic: The Mixtapes He Made for the Girl He Was Wooing
stories.summary: Amit holds up a TDK and a Sony blank tape — mixtapes he made at nineteen for a seventeen-year-old he later married. Making one in those days meant tracking down hard-to-find music, sitting at a double-deck cassette recorder, doing the optimisation math (how many minutes of songs fit on one side), and coordinating playback and recording in real time. Hours of intentional, undivertable effort, all so that one specific person could hear what you loved.
stories.insight: The mixtape was a costly signal in two directions at once: outward, telling the recipient 'this is who I am and I want you to like it,' and inward, forcing the maker to define themselves by curating themselves. Frictionless Spotify playlists transmit the songs perfectly but lose both signals — the labour was the love and the labour was also the self-knowledge.

stories.topic: Writing Letters to a Classmate Two Buildings Away (Ajay)
stories.summary: In Class 8, Ajay and his friend Manisha Purohit sat one desk apart at school and lived two buildings apart in Bandra East — and they began the ritual of writing physical letters to each other and posting them. Sitting at home composing a letter, walking it to the post box, waiting for the reply on paper: a delight that the daily proximity could not replace.
stories.insight: Writing is a different register from talking — slower, more careful, more shaped — and the form invites a kind of attention that no amount of conversation produces. The friends who wrote to each other while sitting together knew, without having read McLuhan, that the medium changes what passes between two people.

stories.topic: How CMIE Was Founded with a Stack of Inland Letters
stories.summary: On 13 April 1976, Ajay's father came home and announced he had been sacked. That same evening he sat down and wrote a stack of inland letters to friends across India saying: I'm starting a new organisation, it'll be called CMIE, here's what I want from you, will you help me. CMIE — now one of India's most important economic data houses — was bootstrapped that night out of handwritten blue paper.
stories.insight: Institutions are built out of trust networks, and trust networks were once literally written by hand. The cost-per-message was high, but the bandwidth-per-message — care, narrative, specific ask — was extraordinarily high too. The modern email or DM has the opposite profile, and we should ask whether we have replaced quality with quantity.

stories.topic: The Locked Godrej Almirah and the Playboys of 1967
stories.summary: Among the unlocked Godrej steel almirahs in Amit's childhood home, one — in his father's study — was always locked. He found the key, opened it, and discovered, among other things, two 1967 Playboys (his father was twenty-five-twenty-six at the time). For a curious teenager in a pre-internet India, in a country that didn't even yet have Debonair, two such magazines were an extraordinary scarce resource — and Amit makes the case that, contra the joke, people genuinely did read Playboy for the stories: Murakami's 'The Second Bakery Attack,' Updike, Cheever, Nabokov, the 20,000-word Larry Page and Sergey Brin Google IPO interview.
stories.insight: Scarcity reshapes the imagination. In a world where the answer to every curiosity is one query away, it is almost impossible to recover the felt weight of a single locked cupboard. And the corollary: the Playboy story tradition is a reminder that high and low never sat in tidy compartments — the prestige short story of the 1980s lived inside an erotic magazine, by editorial design.

stories.topic: The Empty 1986 Diary Began with Tantalizing Tantrums
stories.summary: Each January, Amit's father (a government servant) would receive stacks of free diaries and pass them to twelve-year-old Amit, who wanted to be a writer. Amit holds up the 1986 one. He wrote part of a novel called Tales of St. John's, Chapter One titled 'Tantalizing Tantrums' (already alliterating), in handwriting much better than today's — and then stopped. The diary stayed mostly empty, and stands in for all the writing he never did.
stories.insight: The empty diary is a more honest writer's monument than the filled one — every working writer has a queue of unwritten books. Also: even tossed-aside government diaries were a kind of privilege; a kid in a household without spare paper has no way to put in the volume that turns ambition into craft. Volume requires a sample size, and a sample size requires pages.

stories.topic: The Address Book in the Dining Room as a Material Dunbar Number
stories.summary: Amit produces his mother's old address book — alphabetised but actually chaotic, papers shoved in, numbers scribbled at the back and front. It contained everyone she knew in the world: relatives, friends, the grocer, the electrician, the plumber. It lived in a fixed place in the dining room, and picking it up was a constant tactile reminder that 'these are the people in my life.'
stories.insight: An object that materialises your social network is also an object that asks you, every time you touch it, who you have been intentional about lately. Phones have absorbed the address book and made the question disappear; we now have more contacts and less awareness of them. The map of Dunbar plus has been digitised into invisibility.

stories.topic: Sadhna's Brand-New Diary Every Few Years
stories.summary: Ajay's sister Sadhna kept very high standards of organisation — every few years she would start a fresh diary and methodically migrate the chaos of phone numbers into clean alphabetical pages. Within a year or two, the new diary too would be chaos.
stories.insight: Entropy in the personal-data layer is real and recurrent. Every clean restart eventually accretes mess; the work of organisation is not a one-time project but a permanent low-grade tax. Modern tools defer the entropy but do not abolish it.

stories.summary: Ajay relays a friend's concept of 'one-way journeys' — moments in human history where someone left and you didn't know if they would safely arrive, ever return, or even survive the voyage. No phones, letters that barely worked, real probability of dying in a shipwreck. Today, video calls are ubiquitous, planes are safe, and one-way journeys have effectively vanished.
stories.insight: A huge swath of human emotional life — the goodbye that might be final — has been quietly retired by technology. Many religious and cultural injunctions (e.g. the old Hindu prohibition on overseas travel) are best read as institutional defences against precisely this terror, and they outlive the conditions that produced them.

stories.topic: Creative Animal, Manic Beast, Senile Animal
stories.summary: Amit is not the corporate or networking type, but at MTV they insisted he have a visiting card. Asked for his designation, he refused 'writer' as too boring and got 'Creative Animal' printed instead. Promoted later, he asked: what's a step up from Creative Animal? They gave him 'Manic Beast.' Ajay completes the joke by predicting his retirement card: 'Senile Animal.'
stories.insight: A small but real piece of professional self-definition lived on a 3.5x2-inch piece of card stock. Amit's instinct — to refuse the boring template even when nobody was reading it — is a compact illustration of why aesthetic resistance to the obvious is a low-cost, high-return habit.

stories.topic: Narendra Shenoy's Half-Hour on Michael Porter
stories.summary: Amit's friend Narendra Shenoy, in an arranged marriage, was paired with Sheila — whose talkative twin had been paired with a great conversationalist. Sheila gently asked Narendra whether he had nothing to talk about. Studying for an MBA in another city, calling her from an STD booth and feeling the pressure to be interesting, Narendra spent half an hour explaining the business philosophy of Michael Porter.
stories.insight: A perfect, gentle parable of the STD-booth era: the synchronous, expensive, time-bound long-distance call as an awkward stage on which young people had to perform the new skill of being a partner. The form of the technology shaped not just what was said but who one had to become to say it.

stories.topic: The UP Boy at the STD Booth Saying 'Pranam, Mata Ji'
stories.summary: At the STD booth queue at Ferguson College, a new boy from UP began his call with his mother by intoning 'Pranam, Mata Ji.' Amit, standing at the next booth dialling, heard him and reacted internally with 'What the fuck happened?' — a casual ritual greeting that, in the cosmopolitan college register Amit was used to, sounded almost theatrically formal.
stories.insight: STD booths were not just utilities; they were inadvertent stages where regional registers and class registers collided in public. Compulsory shared phone infrastructure created moments of cultural cross-section that private mobile phones have abolished.

stories.topic: The Badminton Girl Who Rang the Doorbell
stories.summary: Amit, fresh out of a boys' school and unable to read social signals, remembers a girl he used to play badminton with at Ferguson College. One day she rang his doorbell with a friend in tow and asked to use his phone for an urgent call. She made the call and left. It took Amit many years to realise this was almost certainly an expression of interest — a gesture that pre-mobile-phone life uniquely enabled and that he completely missed.
stories.insight: Romantic signalling is partly a function of available infrastructure. The pre-mobile world had its own grammar of gestures (showing up, asking to use the phone, leaving a deliberate trace) that look opaque only to people fluent in the new grammar. Translation between eras is not just possible — it's necessary, or you misread your own past.

stories.summary: Ajay's friend Sushmita tells of the bad old Calcutta phone system: pick up the receiver and you'd hear no dial tone — or, sometimes, somebody else's conversation. One day she lifted the phone and the cross-talk turned out to be two people discussing her.
stories.insight: Infrastructural failure can become a moment of accidental, almost surreal self-revelation. The story is also a reminder of how concretely worse the basic plumbing of life used to be in many parts of India — a baseline modern listeners forget.

stories.topic: The Hostel Pay Phone and Watchman Yelling '262'
stories.summary: At Ajay's IIT Bombay hostel, an entire wing shared one pay phone. To make a call, you queued and dropped a coin. Incoming calls came to the watchman, who would pick up, hear 'I want to speak with Ajay Shah of 262,' and start shouting '262!' across the hostel until the recipient ran down to take the call.
stories.insight: The pay-phone-plus-watchman was a small social institution in itself — a public, semi-mediated communication channel where being phoned was a visible event in the life of the hostel. The vanishing of the institution is also the vanishing of a particular kind of communal awareness of each other's lives.

stories.topic: The Three-Metre Map of India on the Family Wall
stories.summary: Ajay's father bought a four-sheet Survey of India map, built a three-metre-by-three-metre wooden board, and pasted the sheets together to make an enormous wall map of India. Whenever a place name or a river came up in family conversation, the kids would scamper up to the wall to look at it. Ajay laments that he has never been able to find a comparably good wall map of the Himalayas, though he has tried for years (he believes a German company is doing six sheets).
stories.insight: An always-on, room-scale paper map is a different cognitive instrument from any phone or screen — it makes geography ambient, communal, and physically scampered-to. Ajay's failure to recreate it for the Himalayas is a small case study of an obvious-seeming object that is genuinely hard to procure today.

recommendations.item: Sara Rai Inhales Literature (Episode 255, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Sara Rai
recommendations.context: The episode where Sara Rai's astonishing childhood recall set Amit thinking about how scarcity and slowness sharpen observation.
recommendations.reason: Anchor source for the episode's opening provocation — that the absence of constant stimulation is part of why earlier generations seem to remember childhood with novelistic precision.

recommendations.item: Chandrahas Choudhury's Country of Literature (Episode 288, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Chandrahas Choudhury
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with the novelist Chandrahas Choudhury, who still writes long, narrative emails in the manner of letters.
recommendations.reason: The show's living example that letter-style correspondence is still possible in 2024, and that an email can rise to the standard of long-form writing if you choose.

recommendations.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
recommendations.context: Letters Nehru wrote to his daughter Indira from prison, which became a sweeping book on world history.
recommendations.reason: A monument to what handwritten correspondence can become when written with care over time. Amit and Ajay invoke it as a reminder that today's politicians 'do not write letters anymore' — a habit on which whole books once depended.

recommendations.creator: J.R.R. Tolkien
recommendations.context: Tolkien's children's novel, which famously grew out of stories and letters he made for his own children.
recommendations.reason: Paired with Glimpses of World History as another example of how an act of intentional writing within a family — letters and tales told to one's kids — can crystallise into something the world reads forever.

recommendations.item: Playboy Stories: The Best of Forty Years of Short Fiction
recommendations.creator: Edited by Alice K. Turner
recommendations.context: Anthology of literary short stories that originally appeared in Playboy, where Amit first read Murakami, Updike, Cheever and Nabokov.
recommendations.reason: A treasured volume of Amit's, and the evidence behind his claim that Playboy genuinely was a major venue for the best short fiction of the late twentieth century — 'people did read it for the stories.'

recommendations.creator: Larry Page and Sergey Brin (interviewed in Playboy)
recommendations.context: The 20,000-word interview with the Google founders that ran in Playboy at the time of the Google IPO.
recommendations.reason: Concrete proof of how serious the magazine's long-form journalism was: an enormous, substantive interview with the most important tech founders of their generation, run in the same pages as the centrefold.

recommendations.creator: Haruki Murakami
recommendations.context: Murakami's short story; Amit first read it in Playboy.
recommendations.reason: A vivid example, given by name, of how high-prestige literary fiction routinely reached Indian readers via Playboy in the 80s and 90s. (Treated here as a representative work — type 'other' because it is a short story.)

recommendations.item: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
recommendations.creator: Robin Dunbar
recommendations.context: Dunbar's book on the cognitive limits to social-group size — the famous 5/15/50/150 nesting of human relationships.
recommendations.reason: Background source for the address-book-as-Dunbar-plus observation. Useful for thinking about why an ambient physical record of one's network feels right-sized to the human brain.

recommendations.creator: Neil Young
recommendations.context: Slipped in by Ajay as a soft cue between segments.
recommendations.reason: Listed in the show's resources as one of the musical references woven through the episode.

recommendations.item: The Toddy Chicken recipe by Wah Chef
recommendations.creator: Wah Chef
recommendations.context: A YouTube recipe Amit cites as his favourite of the modern, abundant cooking-video genre.
recommendations.reason: Stands in for the cornucopia of free, high-quality cooking instruction that has displaced the painstakingly handwritten family recipe book — a practical example of the trade-off the episode is mapping. (Type 'other' because it is a YouTube recipe video.)

recommendations.item: Narendra Shenoy and Mr Narendra Shenoy (Episode 250, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Narendra Shenoy
recommendations.context: Source episode for the half-hour-on-Michael-Porter STD-booth story.
recommendations.reason: The longer conversation behind the charming arranged-marriage anecdote about a young man trying to fill long-distance silence with management theory.

recommendations.item: Creative destruction (column on the demise of STD booths)
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik
recommendations.context: Ila Patnaik's newspaper column on how mobile roaming wiped out India's STD-booth industry — millions of jobs gone almost overnight.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's go-to text for the argument that job loss in a creatively destructive market economy is mostly not a crisis: India's millions of displaced STD-booth workers found other work, and the country is the better for it.

recommendations.item: Maps Are Magic (Episode 44, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their own earlier episode on the magic of maps.
recommendations.reason: The natural cross-reference for Ajay's lament about the lost strategic feel of paper maps and his hunt for a great wall map of the Himalayas.

recommendations.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
recommendations.context: Borges's one-paragraph fable about a map of an empire so detailed it is the same size as the empire.
recommendations.reason: Amit's joke punchline to Ajay's quest for the perfect Himalayan wall map: any truly accurate map of the Himalayas would have to be as big as the Himalayas.

recommendations.creator: The Replacements
recommendations.context: The Replacements' early-1980s album, which Amit calls the best album titled Let It Be (with the Beatles in second place).
recommendations.reason: The home of 'Answering Machine' — and a chance for Amit to make his cheerful, contrarian case for The Replacements over the Beatles on the question of who owns that album title.

recommendations.creator: The Replacements
recommendations.context: Song from The Replacements' Let It Be, with the line 'How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?'
recommendations.reason: A poignant museum-piece of a lyric: the kind of pathos available only when the answering machine still existed as a felt object — and a line whose pathos is now lost on a generation that has never seen one.

recommendations.item: Vitalik Buterin Fights the Dragon-Tyrant (Episode 342, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vitalik Buterin
recommendations.context: The Madras conversation in which Buterin spoke with Amit and Ajay about the underappreciated value of cash.
recommendations.reason: Source for Ajay's closing case for cash: anonymity, universal acceptance, and freedom from the surveillance world a fully-electronic payment regime creates.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their online course, in which one of the assignments is daily private journaling on assigned subjects.
recommendations.reason: Plugged in service of the larger argument that writing privately, daily, and unfiltered is one of the most underused tools for self-knowledge — Joan Didion's 'I don't know what I think until I write it down,' operationalised.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's standard-reference book on Indian economic policy, listed in the show resources.
recommendations.reason: The ambient reference text Amit and Ajay link to throughout the series — relevant here as the home of arguments about creative destruction and market economies that Ajay invokes when discussing the STD-booth wipeout.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's online writing course, listed in the show resources.
recommendations.reason: Linked in the resources because the episode's central claim about letters and journaling — that writing is shaping, not just expressing — is the foundation of the course.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's Substack newsletter, listed in the show resources.
recommendations.reason: Standing recommendation; relevant to this episode's pitch that long-form writing — letters, essays, even emails treated as letters — is a virtue worth keeping alive.

core_ideas.concept: We Shape Our Objects, Then Our Objects Shape Us
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's framing for the whole episode: an object's significance is rarely just its function. Around each object grows an entire culture of behaviour — making mixtapes, walking to the post box, queueing at an STD booth, scampering up to a wall map. When the object disappears, the world it organised disappears with it, and we mostly notice only in retrospect. The exercise of the episode is to be self-aware in the present that some object you handle today is being used by you for the last time, even if you don't know it yet.
core_ideas.quote: We shape our objects and then our objects shape us in ways that go far beyond the simple functionality.

core_ideas.explanation: Mixtapes, handwritten letters, posted inland letters, STD-booth calls — all required real time and friction, and that friction was the message. The labour told the recipient 'I care about this and about you' in a way that no zero-cost click can. The episode's recurring claim is not that we should reject frictionless communication, but that we should consciously pay attention with the new tools — because the old tools used to compel attention by virtue of their cost.
core_ideas.quote: It demands effort and attention and focus. We harnessed the CPU seconds of the mind into doing this and that created beauty and it shaped us in ways that many people in today's world don't quite know.

core_ideas.concept: Writing as Shaping, Not Just Expressing
core_ideas.explanation: From Joan Didion: 'I don't know what I think until I write it down.' The act of writing is not a transparent broadcast of pre-existing thought; it is the process by which thought becomes thought. This is why Amit and Ajay urge daily, private, unfiltered journaling — and why they think the modern decline of letter-writing is a loss not just of correspondence but of self-construction. Writing by hand, slower and uneditable, raises the bar still higher: the brain power going in is of a higher order than on a modern keyboard.
core_ideas.quote: When you write, you're not only expressing yourself, you are shaping yourself.

core_ideas.concept: The Long-Form Email as Surviving Letter
core_ideas.explanation: Both hosts argue that email can be the modern letter — if you treat it as one. Gmail's drafts folder lets you edit a single email for days; you don't have to hit send. Lant Pritchett and Ajay write each other 3,000-word emails with month-long reply turnarounds. A subject line of 'long-form, X' is a useful flag to the reader that this isn't a transactional ping. The technology has not killed the form; the social default has — and the default is fixable.
core_ideas.quote: You are not obliged to punch send right there. It is stored in a folder that is called drafts.

core_ideas.concept: Asynchronous Messaging as a New Frame of Mind
core_ideas.explanation: Before mobile phones, communication was either nothing (you waited to meet someone) or fully synchronous (you both stood at phones with the meter running). Modern messaging on Signal or WhatsApp introduced a third regime — asynchronous text — and that regime carries its own social grammar: the recipient is probably not seeing it now, the conversation is layered across hours and days, and the bar for what is worth sending has dropped to near zero ('did you take your meds today'). This is genuinely new, not just faster.
core_ideas.quote: Asynchronous messaging is a very different frame of mind compared to either nothing or synchronous.

core_ideas.concept: The Address Book as Material Dunbar Number
core_ideas.explanation: Robin Dunbar's research suggests human social cognition tops out around 150 close-ish relationships, nested inside circles of 50, 15 and 5. The mid-twentieth-century household address book, kept in a fixed place and touched daily, was a physical instantiation of that universe — picking it up was a tactile reminder of who one was actually connected to. Smartphones have absorbed and obscured the function. We now have many more contacts, and far less awareness of the shape of our network.

For most of human history, leaving was sometimes final. People departed by road or sea with no phones, unreliable letters, real chance of dying en route — and goodbyes carried the possibility of being last goodbyes. Modern airplane travel and ubiquitous video calls have effectively retired the one-way journey from ordinary life. A whole register of grief, anxiety and ritual has gone with it; many cultural and religious injunctions (e.g. the old Hindu prohibition on overseas travel) read as fossils of that vanished emotional regime.
core_ideas.quote: In today's world there are no one-way journeys.

core_ideas.concept: Religions as Mirrors of the Mores They Emerged From
core_ideas.explanation: Many religious injunctions read more cleanly as practical responses to specific historical conditions: the prohibition on pork as a protection against undercooked-meat illness; the prohibition on overseas travel as a defence against losing one's young to a one-way journey. Once embedded in religion, these rules become harder to revise as conditions change — which is why we still inherit them long after the original danger has gone.

core_ideas.concept: Privilege Shows Up at the Level of Paper
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's reflection on his stack of free 1986 government diaries leads him to a usually-invisible point about privilege: in many households, having any paper at all to write in was scarce. You can't develop as a writer without volume — without enough iterations to build a sample size — and you can't put in the volume without raw material. Writers get made not just by talent but by access to pages.
core_ideas.quote: If you're not actually writing, writing, writing, writing a lot, writing so much that it can be thrown away, you don't really have anything.

core_ideas.concept: Scarcity as a Multiplier of Value (and Danger of Paralysis)
core_ideas.explanation: When notebooks were rare, every page mattered, and the writer cared. The same logic applies across the episode's objects — a single Playboy carried more imaginative weight than the entire internet does today; a single STD-booth call had to mean something. But scarcity has a shadow: when pages are too precious, perfection becomes the enemy of production and the would-be writer freezes. The right amount of friction is somewhere between zero and so much that nothing gets made.

core_ideas.concept: Borges's Map: Why Perfect Fidelity Is Impossible
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay laments that he can't find a wall map detailed enough for the Himalayas. Amit invokes Borges's parable of the map of the empire that is the same size as the empire itself: any map is a deliberate compression, and trying to escape that compression collapses the very point of mapping. Modern Google Maps has a different problem — its legending is optimised for screens, not walls, so even at 40 inches it cannot recover the strategic-overview feel of an old Bartholomew or National Geographic sheet. Different forms of compression yield different forms of insight.
core_ideas.quote: The only accurate map of the Himalayas would have to be as big as the Himalayas.

core_ideas.concept: Creative Destruction in the Indian Labour Market
core_ideas.explanation: The death of STD booths displaced more than a million Indian workers almost overnight, but, Ajay argues following Ila Patnaik, this was not the catastrophe it sounds like. A creatively destructive market economy reabsorbs displaced labour into new sectors; STD-booth operators moved on. The episode's broader point — important for anyone reflexively gloomy about job loss from automation or technology — is that 'job loss' and 'human suffering' are not the same variable, and India's experience is largely on the optimistic side of the ledger.

Ajay's closing pitch: cash is a public good worth defending. Its acceptance is universal, its anonymity is real, and once you replace it entirely with electronic payments, you have built a panopticon by accident — every transaction traceable, every citizen permanently legible to the state. He cites his Madras conversation with Vitalik Buterin and the dystopian example of China, where the cash infrastructure has actually broken down. Using cash, in this frame, is a small act of civic responsibility.

Ajay's modernised proposal: instead of paper cards, encode a URL pointing to your VCF (vCard) file as a QR code. Google Contacts will periodically poll the URL, so updates to your details propagate automatically into other people's address books. It's the rare case where the digital version of a vanished object isn't just frictionless but strictly better — the contact never goes stale.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay opens with a hoarse voice, Amit gestures to a giant bag, and Ajay deadpans: 'I have a new voice for you in my bag, so in case your voice goes — we have no, no, I'm just kidding.'
Amit on his unused mixtape-era ambition: 'As far as people you are wooing is concerned, 100% strike rate.'

Ajay deadpans about the typewriter as the half-way house between pen and computer: 'There's no backspace there. So if you make too many mistakes, you gotta type it again, and if you have one or two mistakes, then you'll take a black ink and you'll do all kinds of random things over there.'

On finding two 1967 Playboys in his father's locked Godrej almirah, Amit calculates that his father was twenty-five — so the magazines may have been his twenty-sixth birthday present, 'coming a little, sort of, delayed.'
Amit, on Playboy's literary pedigree: 'There's this old saying where people will joke, I read Playboy for the stories. Now, the thing is — they actually did.'
Amit on his teenage daughter being 'underaged for psychedelic drugs': 'Nobody nobody is underage for psychedelic drugs. So I've never had any. I'm just saying random things.'

Amit's MTV visiting cards: he refused 'writer' as too boring and got 'Creative Animal' printed; promoted later, he asked for the next step up and got 'Manic Beast.' Ajay supplies the unwritten retirement card: 'Senile Animal.'

On young Narendra Shenoy filling a long-distance call to his fiancee with management theory: 'For half an hour, he tells her about the business philosophy of Michael Porter. So I mean, this is what boys were like.'

On STD-booth posturing: a new boy from UP at Ferguson College begins his call with 'Pranam, Mata Ji,' which Amit, dialling at the next booth, hears as so theatrically formal that his internal reaction is 'What the fuck happened?'

Ajay's blanket judgment of the bad old Calcutta phone system: 'There is India and then there is Calcutta. Everything is worse in Calcutta. What Bengal thinks today, the rest of India hopes will never happen to them.'
Sushmita's Calcutta crossed-line story: she picks up the phone, hears a stranger conversation, and realises the two people on the line are talking about her.
Amit's contrarian rock canon: 'Great song by a band called The Replacements, who had the best album called Let It Be. The Beatles are in second place.'

On the gulf between generations: 'How do you say goodnight to an answering machine?' — a Replacements lyric whose pathos, Amit notes, is now lost on a generation who'd ask 'What the fuck is an answering machine?'
Amit on the modern recipe abundance: 'Today, recipes are a dime a dozen. You go on YouTube — cooking videos are a dime a dozen. My favourite of course being Toddy Chicken.'
Joan Didion: 'I don't know what I think until I write it down' — invoked as the case for daily journaling and for treating writing as an act of self-construction, not transcription.
Robin Dunbar's number(s) — 5/15/50/150 — invoked to describe the address book as 'Dunbar plus,' since it included not only one's 150 social contacts but also the grocer, electrician, and plumber.

Glimpses of World History (Nehru's letters from prison to Indira) and The Hobbit (which grew out of Tolkien's letters to his children) — invoked together as cases of letter-writing that became literature.
Borges's 'On Exactitude in Science' — Amit's punchline to Ajay's hunt for the perfect Himalayan wall map: 'The only accurate map of the Himalayas would have to be as big as the Himalayas.'
Neil Young, 'After the Gold Rush' — slipped in by Ajay as a music cue between segments.
Vitalik Buterin in Madras — quoted approvingly by Ajay on how dystopian fully-electronic payment systems become; 'cash is freedom' is the closing line.

Ila Patnaik's column on the demise of STD booths — Ajay's standing example of how a creatively destructive market economy in India can wipe out an entire million-strong industry without producing a labour-market crisis.
